title: Cluster-configurational study of G-center in Silicon
authors: Narayan Pokhrel, Kyungwha Park, Vsevolod Ivanov
abstract: Understanding the properties of defects is imperative for proper use for variety of applications including quantum computing. In this paper, we use the multiconfigurational self consistent field (MCSCF) combined with DFT optimized geometry in order to investigate the spin and optical properties of G centers in Silicon. By utilizing quantum chemistry based methods, we show excellent agreement with the Zero Phonon Line and Zero Field Splitting Tensor components of the G center. We also calculate the theoretical spin decoherence time of the G centers using Cluster Correlation Expansion (CCE) methods.
summary: This paper theoretically characterizes the G-center defect in Silicon, a promising platform for quantum computing. Using advanced multiconfigurational quantum chemistry methods, the authors calculate key properties like ZPL energy, Zero Field Splitting, and spin decoherence times. The results validate the use of complex electronic structure calculations to predict solid-state qubit performance.
main_problem: The study investigates the spin and optical properties of G-centers defects in Silicon, which are critical components for potential quantum computing applications.
main_result: The theoretical calculations show excellent agreement with Zero Phonon Line energies and Zero Field Splitting components, and estimate a substantial spin decoherence time (1.465 ms).
method: The research employs advanced quantum chemistry methods including Multiconfigurational Self-Consistent Field (MCSCF), CASSCF(6,6), NEVPT2 corrections, and Cluster Correlation Expansion (CCE) for coherence time.
model_or_system: The physical system is the G-center defect embedded in Silicon. The calculations model this using various supercell sizes (up to 512 atoms) and focus on the electronic structure of the singlet ($S=0$) and triplet ($S=1$) manifolds.
key_observables: Zero Phonon Line (ZPL) energy ($\approx 0.969$ eV), Zero Field Splitting components ($D_{xx}, D_{yy}, D_{zz}$), theoretical spin decoherence time ($T_2$), and Transition Dipole Moment (TDM).
important_parameters: The active space size is systematically expanded from CAS(2,2) to CAS(6,6); the calculations are sensitive to cluster size convergence.
main_assumptions: The multiconfigurational approach is necessary because single-configuration wavefunctions fail for describing the optical excitation process; approximations are made in calculating spin-vibrational coupling and decoherence rates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the G-center structure, the detailed computational workflow (from supercell relaxation to CASSCF), and energy level diagrams showing relative positions of singlet and triplet states.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the necessity of multiconfigurational methods for defect centers. It details a rigorous computational workflow involving geometry optimization, CASSCF calculations across increasing active spaces, and finally applying CCE/PYCCE to predict spin coherence times.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the theoretical modeling required for solid-state qubits by providing detailed predictions of optical transitions (ZPL) and spin coherence times ($T_2$) based on first principles quantum chemistry.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of the G-center structure and electronic states. The G-center structure has (C1h) symmetry consisting of two substitutinal carbon atoms (black spheres) in silicon (blue spheres). The electronic structure consists of a singlet (S = 0) ground and excited states and a metastable triplet (S = 1) state. Primary multiconfigurational components of each state are shown in terms of the localized orbital basis.

Fig. 2 Overview of the computational workflow. The G-center structure is relaxed within a 512-atom supercell using a hybrid functional approach. From this structure, hydrogen-passivated structures are obtained: Model 1 (69 atoms), Model 2 (141 atoms), and Model 3 (265 atoms). Electronic structures for these models are obtained using a 2-orbital + 2-electron CASSCF (2,2) calculation from which the six-orbital basis is obtained through a Pipek-Mezey localization procedure. These orbitals are then used for the full-scale 6-electron + 6-orbital CASSCF (6,6) calculation, followed by NEVPT2 corrections and postprocessing to obtain spin properties.

Fig. 3 Top view of the 6 defect orbitals in the SA-CASSCF calculation of 69 atom cluster ordered according to energy. Similar 6 active orbitals are present for 141 and 265 atom structure. The AVO- GADRO [41] program is used for visualization.
Fig. 4 Energy diagram showing the relative position of Singlets and Triplets in SA-CASSCF calculations. The inset show the level splitting of the triplet level by SOC and SOC+SSC
